DESIGN: A pilot block randomized controlled trial over 12 weeks. Participants were randomized to the intervention (Paro) or control condition (standard care). SETTING: Two dementia day care centers and participants' homes in Auckland, New Zealand. PARTICIPANTS: Thirty dyads (consisting of a care recipient with dementia and their caregiver) took part in this study. All care recipients attended dementia day care centers at Selwyn Foundation and had a formal diagnosis of dementia. INTERVENTION: Thirty-minute unstructured group sessions with Paro at the day care center were run 2 to 3 times a week for 6 weeks. Participants also had Paro at home for 6 weeks. MEASUREMENTS: At the day care centers, observations of the care recipients' behavior, affect, and social responses were recorded using a time sampling method. Observations of interactions with Paro for participants in the intervention were also recorded. Blood pressure and salivary cortisol were collected from care recipients before and after sessions at day care. In the home setting, level of cognition, depressive symptoms, neuropsychiatric symptoms, behavioral agitation, and blood pressure were measured at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks. Hair cortisol measures were collected at baseline and at 6 weeks. RESULTS: Observations showed that Paro significantly improved facial expressions (affect) and communication with staff (social interaction) at the day care centers. Subanalyses showed that care recipients with less cognitive impairment responded significantly better to Paro. text:
# Social robots used with older people: a map of the evidence

This map covers studies where a robot was actually used with older people. I left out studies that only surveyed attitudes, ran focus groups, or showed robot videos. Most of what follows comes from abstracts, not full texts, so check details against the papers before citing them.

## 1. Overview

- **The evidence is mostly small and short.** Reviews describe a literature with many positive reports but weak methods.
  - A scoping review covered 33 studies, 1,574 participants and 11 robots. 28 of the 33 reported positive findings, but many had methodological problems [W2789445850]. It grouped the robots' roles into affective therapy, cognitive training, social facilitator, companionship and physiological therapy.
  - A meta-analysis of RCTs found 11 trials, of which 9 were pooled. Agitation, anxiety and quality of life trended positive but were not statistically significant. Narrative synthesis suggested benefits for engagement, interaction, stress indicators, loneliness and medication use. Risk of bias was high, especially for allocation concealment and blinding [W2808281222].
  - A review of depression found 7 studies (6 RCTs). Three showed promising reductions and three showed non-significant downward trends. The authors judged the evidence too weak to recommend the approach clinically [W2889960145].
- **One robot dominates.** Most controlled work uses PARO, a robotic seal, with people who have dementia in care facilities. Humanoid, mobile and telepresence robots are mostly tested in feasibility or field studies.

## 2. Robots, participants and settings

### A. Animal-like robots (PARO, AIBO, robotic cats and pets)

| Study | Robot | Participants / setting | Design | Main findings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [W1488883230] | PARO | 18 residents with mid- to late-stage dementia, one aged-care facility in Australia | Pilot randomized crossover vs reading group | Moderate-to-large positive effect on quality of life; higher pleasure scores. The authors call for a larger trial. |
| [W2778691880] | PARO | Long-term care residents with dementia | Cluster RCT vs plush toy and usual care. This paper is a qualitative follow-up on 5 participants. | Responses varied widely between people and within the same person over time. The authors raise ethical issues about giving PARO and taking it back. The trial's quantitative results are reported elsewhere, and I didn't retrieve them. |
| [W3088196398] | PARO | 60 residents with dementia, 10 Norwegian nursing homes | Cluster RCT: 30 minutes twice weekly for 12 weeks, group activity | Better sleep (efficiency, total sleep time, fewer awakenings), measured with wrist actigraphy. |
| [W2732925385] | PARO | 30 dyads of people with dementia and caregivers; two day-care centres and homes in New Zealand | Pilot block RCT, 12 weeks | Better facial affect and communication with staff at day care. Responses were stronger in people with less cognitive impairment. No differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures. |
| [W3015603533] | PARO | 20 older adults with depression, 4 long-term care facilities in Taiwan. Each kept PARO 24/7 for 8 weeks. | Single-group before/after, with interviews | Depression and loneliness fell and quality of life rose during the intervention stage but not during the earlier observation stage. There was no control group. |
| [W1807810766] | PARO, NAO and a real dog | 101 and 110 nursing home residents in two phases, plus 20 and 17 day-care patients, with dementia | Non-randomized parallel arms, 2 days a week for 3 months | Apathy improved in the robot groups. The NAO group's MMSE scores declined, though the sMMSE did not. Quality-of-life (QUALID) scores rose in the PARO group. In day care, irritability and total NPI improved in phase 1 only. |
| [W2132164645] | AIBO and a live dog | Long-term care facility residents | Comparison with a no-therapy control | Both dog and robot groups had less loneliness than controls. Residents became attached to both, but attachment did not explain the loneliness change. |
| [W3015009700] | Joy for All robot animals (low-cost) | Two supported-living sites, for people with dementia or learning difficulties | Six-month diary study | Use grew from short structured sessions to near-permanent availability, so novelty did not fade. Reported benefits were reminiscence, communication and possibly less agitation. Some people called the robots "creepy". |

Observational PARO studies in nursing homes include:
- Group sensory therapy with residents who had dementia [W2040979576, W4243437205].
- A three-month naturalistic field study [W2039822570].
- A study of how staff, residents and visitors reshape what PARO is used for [W2043587319].

Infection control is a practical issue. One paper assessed microbial contamination and disinfection of companion robots in care homes [W3081435517].

I found these but did not read their results, so treat them as leads:
- A comparison of responses to a visiting person with a dog, a robot seal and a toy cat [W2294211165].
- Verbal and emotional responses by dementia severity [W1505024467].
- A PARO pain pilot RCT [W3097289914].
- A PARO and sleep paper from the same Norwegian group [W3102212853].

### B. Humanoid and conversational robots

- **Brian 2.1** was an expressive humanoid used as a mealtime motivator at a care facility with 8 people aged 82–93. They engaged with it and complied with its prompts, and they rated it positively [W2112421347]. The same group's earlier work covered a memory game in a long-term care facility [W2003566851].
- **Robot exercise coaches.** Fasola and Matarić tested a relational robot coach against a non-relational one. Participants strongly preferred the relational coach for enjoyment, companionship and coaching [W2065178260].
- **Conversational and assessment robots.**
  - A conversational robot was piloted with people who have Alzheimer's disease [W3033476063].
  - A social robot administered cognitive tests to community-dwelling older adults, and reliability and acceptability were examined [W2924547041].
  - A social robot collected patient-reported outcome measures from older patients in hospital [W2946005838].
  - A chat robot, "Sunshine", was piloted in long-term care during COVID-19 [W3041860695].
- **Participatory-arts and mood work.** NAO was used with theatre-based activities in residential care [W2982896790, W2899915867]. A robot was also used to promote human-to-human connection in an assisted-living community [W2943699887].
- **Ethics-focused longitudinal study.** In two retirement villages, older adults had 8 sessions over 4 weeks with a robot that was either emotive or non-emotive. Attachment was low to medium, and the robot's behaviour did not change acceptance. Perceived ease of use rose over time [W3001702224].
- **Care-home deployments.** A 12-week non-randomized trial put six health-care robots in an aged-care facility, with 53 residents and 53 staff. It found no major benefits or problems. Perceived agency of the robots fell over time [W1945345301]. The Zora robot (a NAO with software) was evaluated over two years in 14 Dutch care organizations [W2915888239]. I did not read its findings.
- **Humanoid robot versus tablet training for people with dementia at home.** I found only the study protocol [W2975531399].

### C. Mobile service and companion robots in homes

- **Hobbit** was tested for multiple weeks in 16 private homes of people aged 75 and over. All users interacted with it daily, rated most functions as working well, and thought it would be part of future elderly care. Its adaptive behaviour eased interaction over time. Real-home trials exposed problems such as misinterpreted actions during unscripted interaction [W2994761079]. An earlier trial ran in 18 households [W3137166629], and a German-language paper describes the field-trial experience [W2402706188].
- **A voice-driven companion robot** was tested with 8 older adults living alone, who each used it for about 95 days. Navigation and verbal communication were the most useful functions but also the least reliable. Users accepted it enthusiastically, but speech recognition and navigation need work [W2717439789].
- **A robot walking-group assistant** was deployed for a month with two weekly walking groups for older adults with advanced dementia. Therapists saw potential gains in motivation, group coherence and mood, and residents were curious and open. Technical problems quickly turned the robot into extra workload for the therapists [W4251569456].
- **A relational-agent robot** gave social support to isolated older adults [W2130723705]. The MARIO companion robot was deployed in a nursing home for people with dementia [W2896071495, W2889731820]. I only saw abstract-level material for these.

### D. Telepresence robots

- GIRAFF/ROBIN long-term evaluations targeted older people living at home [W2259814160, W2394797369, W2743226003].
- Usability and attitude work involved older adults with mobility impairment [W2592259105, W2593419711].
- An integrative review looked at telepresence for people with dementia [W2751864896].
- These are mostly feasibility and usability studies. I did not retrieve outcome data.

## 3. What the studies suggest

1. **Affective and social engagement is the most consistent finding.** PARO and similar robots reliably produce engagement, positive affect and social interaction in observational and pilot studies [W2732925385, W1488883230, W2040979576].
2. **Clinical outcomes are mixed.** Dementia symptoms and physiological measures often did not differ from controls [W2732925385], and meta-analytic effects were not significant [W2808281222]. The most robust-looking positive result is sleep in a cluster RCT [W3088196398]. Depression and loneliness results come largely from uncontrolled or small designs [W3015603533].
3. **Responses vary between people.** Effects depend on dementia severity [W2732925385] and differ even within one person over time [W2778691880]. The NAO arm in [W1807810766] shows that not every robot arm improved.
4. **Novelty may not be the main problem.** In the six-month diary study, robot use increased over time [W3015009700]. In the Hobbit and Companion field tests, the main barriers were reliability and robustness, not lack of interest [W2994761079, W2717439789, W4251569456].
5. **Several robots, no clear benefit.** The multi-robot aged-care trial found neither benefits nor harms [W1945345301]. This suggests the robot's role and fit matter more than having a robot present.
6. **Controls are inconsistent.** Studies used plush toys, reading groups, live dogs or usual care, so comparisons across studies are hard.

## 4. Gaps

- There is little evidence on healthy or independent older adults. Most controlled work involves dementia.
- Home-based trials are small, and long-term trials of humanoid robots are rare.
- Few studies use blinded outcome assessment or adequate sample sizes.
- Robots other than PARO are under-evaluated in controlled designs.
- Ethics (deception, attachment, withdrawal) is studied less than efficacy [W3001702224, W2778691880].

## 5. Limits of this search

These came from keyword searches of a database, not a complete systematic search. I didn't search specifically for Pepper, ElliQ, Jibo, Tega or Kompaï, and I may have missed trials, especially recent ones. I can run a targeted search on any robot, population (for example MCI or healthy older adults), or setting (home or hospital). I can also pull the full results of the trials I flagged as leads.
Keep only studies with people living with dementia, and add any relevant ones you missed.

text:
# Social robots with people living with dementia

I narrowed the set to studies where people with dementia used a robot. I also ran new searches on dementia, Alzheimer's disease, robot pets and humanoids, and on reminiscence and music, and read the abstracts of about 30 more candidates.

**Dropped from the earlier map:**
- Studies of general older adults, healthy seniors, depression-only samples, or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) only. These included the Hobbit, home-companion, Brian 2.1 mealtime, exercise-coach, telepresence and ethics studies.
- The AIBO loneliness study [W2132164645], the Taiwanese PARO depression study [W3015603533] and the multi-robot aged-care trial [W1945345301], because none of them specified dementia.
- The general reviews, because they pool non-dementia studies.

## 1. Controlled and comparative studies

| Study | Robot | Participants and setting | Design | Findings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [W3088196398] | PARO | 60 residents with dementia, 10 Norwegian nursing home special care units | Cluster RCT: 30 minutes twice weekly for 12 weeks, vs treatment as usual | Better sleep efficiency and total sleep time, fewer awakenings (wrist actigraphy). |
| [W3097289914] | PARO | 43 residents with dementia and chronic pain, 3 Australian nursing homes | Pilot RCT: individual non-facilitated 30-minute sessions, 5 days a week for 6 weeks | Lower observed pain (PAINAD) and fewer as-needed medications than usual care. No difference in staff-rated pain or scheduled medications. This is a conference abstract. |
| [W2732925385], [W2995685337] | PARO | 30 dyads in two day-care centres and homes, New Zealand. The thesis reports 28 dyads. | Pilot block RCT, 12 weeks | Better facial affect and communication with staff at day care. No differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures. People with less cognitive impairment responded better. Caregiver stress and burden also showed limited effects [W2995685337]. |
| [W1488883230] | PARO | 18 residents with mid- to late-stage dementia, one Australian facility | Randomized crossover vs reading group | Moderate-to-large improvement in quality of life and higher pleasure scores. |
| [W2778691880] | PARO | Long-term care residents with dementia | Cluster RCT vs plush toy and usual care. This paper is a qualitative follow-up on 5 participants. | Responses varied between people and within one person over time. It raises ethical issues about giving PARO and taking it back. |
| [W2894885829] | PARO | 33 nursing home residents with dementia (17 intervention, 16 control), Korea | Non-equivalent control group, 12 sessions over 6 weeks | Better positive emotion and social interaction, and fewer problem behaviours. |
| [W1807810766] | PARO, NAO and a real dog | 101 and 110 nursing home residents (two phases), plus 20 and 17 day-care patients | Non-randomized parallel arms, 2 days a week for 3 months | Apathy improved in the robot groups. The NAO group's MMSE declined, though its severe-impairment score (sMMSE) did not. QUALID quality-of-life scores rose with PARO in phase 2. Day-care results were mixed. |
| [W1505024467] | PARO vs stuffed lion | 19 residents with mild or moderate dementia and 11 with severe dementia, Japan | Within-subject comparison, 6 minutes of video-coded interaction | Both groups talked to PARO more, laughed more and showed more positive emotion than with the toy. Staff talked more with mild/moderate residents when the toy was used. |
| [W2294211165] | PARO, live dog, toy cat | 100 nursing home residents completed 12 visits. Dementia diagnoses were recorded, but the sample was not limited to dementia. | RCT | Dog and PARO prompted the most interaction. PARO's effect faded over time. |
| [W1972564462] | AIBO, live dog, visitor alone | Female nursing home residents with dementia | Comparative visits | Both the dog and AIBO increased social interaction beyond the visitor alone. AIBO produced longer looks and more resident-initiated conversation than the dog. |
| [W2074069593] | Robotic cat vs plush cat | Special care unit in a nursing home | Pilot with direct observation | Similar trends for both cats: less agitation, more pleasure and interest. |
| [W4407738599] | PARO vs stuffed animal | Patients with dementia in occupational therapy | Comparison (abstract only) | Authors concluded the robot differs from an inert toy and encouraged more self-directed behaviour. |

## 2. Observational, feasibility and qualitative studies

**PARO**
- **Group sensory therapy.** Ten residents, weekly sessions. Physical interaction and willingness to engage rose steadily over the study, which argues against a novelty effect [W2040979576, W4243437205].
- **Three-month field study.** PARO was placed in a public area of a nursing home. Staff and family mediation was key to successful interaction [W2039822570].
- **Single session.** Eleven community-dwelling older adults with MCI or mild-to-moderate dementia took part. Participants stayed focused on PARO and many talked to it as if it were a pet. Mood improved but not significantly [W2080233792].
- **Pain and mood interviews.** Residents with chronic pain reported better mood and relaxation, and some anecdotal pain relief. They also noted PARO's weight and voice as limits [W2985514812].
- **Care-provider views.** In a study of care providers (not residents), staff said PARO's sounds can overstimulate [W2689483015].

**Other robots**
- **MARIO** is a companion robot with music, news, reminiscence, games and calendar apps.
  - Ten residents, 4 weeks, up to 12 sessions, Irish nursing home. They stayed interested and spent more time socially engaged. Quality of life, depression and perceived social support did not change significantly [W2955051104].
  - Multiple case study: resilience was supported in 8 of 10 people, but they needed skilled facilitation [W3092218325].
  - Interviews with people with dementia, carers and managers in the UK, Italy and Ireland were mostly positive. Voice recognition was a problem, and some staff feared robots would replace them [W3105249390, W2896071495, W2889731820].
- **Matilda and similar baby-face humanoids** in Australian residential care.
  - One study coded over 11,000 reactions from 139 residents across 5 years. It reports sensory enrichment, positive engagement and entertainment [W2317990020].
  - A trial with 115 participants reports significant gains in emotional, visual and behavioural engagement over the years, and acceptance [W2564685734].
  - Betty was studied in home care with people with dementia. It reports engagement and a need for personalization, with no quantitative detail in the abstract [W2944083468].
- **Ryan Companionbot** is a conversational, life-like robot. Six people with moderate dementia and/or depression had it in their rooms 24/7 for 4–6 weeks. They built rapport and valued it [W2771925981].
- **Conversational robot for Alzheimer's disease.** A cognitive assessment pilot. Conversations were better with humans, but participants liked the robot and stayed interested despite miscommunication [W3033476063].
- **Walking-group robot.** Adults with advanced dementia, a month of use. Therapists reported gains in motivation, group coherence and mood, but technical faults added to their workload [W4251569456]. In a companion analysis, most interaction was prompted by therapists, and only 2 of 12 residents initiated any [W2592905630].
- **Robot cat at home.** A qualitative case study of people with dementia living at home. Benefits appeared where the cat was accepted, and some people rejected it [W3034490183].
- **Robotic animal companions.** Two qualitative studies, one comparing a live dog with a robot in a care home and one longitudinal single case. The authors conclude robots can enrich social and emotional life [W3198896322].

## 3. Reviews specific to dementia
- A systematic review of dogs and robotic animals in nursing homes (15 articles) found:
  - Behavioural and psychological symptoms were reduced in 6 of 11 studies.
  - Depression or mood improved in 6 of 9.
  - Quality of life improved in 3 of 5.
  - Dogs and robot animals were combined, so it can't isolate the robot effect [W2946010724].
- A telepresence-for-dementia review exists [W2751864896]. I didn't read it in full.

## 4. What the dementia studies suggest
1. **PARO dominates and has the strongest controlled evidence.** The newest RCTs tested clinical outcomes: sleep and pain/medication [W3088196398, W3097289914].
2. **Short-term engagement and affect are the most consistent results** across designs and robots [W1505024467, W2894885829, W2732925385].
3. **Symptom and quality-of-life results are mixed.** Some trials find no change in dementia symptoms or standardized scales [W2732925385, W2955051104]. In the multi-arm study, NAO's cognition result was worse [W1807810766].
4. **Response varies with severity and person.** Milder cognitive impairment predicted better responses in one trial [W2732925385]. Another found responses changed within the same person [W2778691880].
5. **Facilitation matters.** Staff mediation drove interaction in PARO, MARIO and walking-group studies [W2039822570, W3092218325, W2592905630].
6. **Novelty effects were not clearly seen.** Interaction grew over weeks in the PARO group studies [W2040979576]. However, PARO's effect faded over 12 visits in another [W2294211165].
7. **Practical issues.** Robot weight, voice and sound, voice recognition, and system reliability came up repeatedly [W2985514812, W3105249390, W4251569456].

## 5. Borderline or unread items
- **Mixed populations:** Joy for All robot animals used for six months at supported-living sites for people with dementia or learning difficulties [W3015009700]. The 14-person apathy study (robot games with pairs of residents) was mostly MCI, with one person with Alzheimer's [W3113108394]. An AIBO study with early cognitive deficits (MMSE above 23, so mostly not dementia) [W2159536297]. These did not meet a strict dementia criterion.
- **Protocol only, no results:** humanoid robot versus tablet training for people with dementia at home [W2975531399].
- **Abstract only or too thin to use:**
  - A thesis on the PARO cluster RCT covering agitation, depression, psychotropic drug use and quality of life. The abstract gives no results [W3102212853].
  - A MiRo animal-robot development abstract [W2895915058].
  - A robot music therapist for cognitive impairment, with no study details [W759765632].
  - Recreational communication robots in nursing homes [W2585556435].
- **Not checked:** I hit the tool-call limit before fetching one more candidate, a 3-month PARO field study. The tool lists many older Japanese PARO studies (2004–2006) whose participants are "elderly" without dementia specified. Checking these may add dementia studies.

## 6. Gaps
- Almost all robots studied are PARO or similar animal robots. Controlled evidence on humanoid, conversational or mobile robots with people with dementia is thin.
- Home and community studies are small or qualitative.
- Many studies are short, unblinded and have small samples, and a few are non-randomized.
- Dementia severity and subtype are inconsistently reported, even though response seems to depend on them.

I can fetch full texts for the trials most relevant to you, or search specifically for caregiver outcomes, home-based dementia studies, or non-PARO robots.
Which papers from your first map did you drop, and why?

Below is every paper I cited in the first map that isn't in the dementia-only version. Some were dropped for a clear reason, but for others I just couldn't confirm the population. I also found an error in my last message, which I've put at the end.

## A. Dropped because the participants were not people with dementia
These abstracts name a different group, such as healthy seniors, depression-only samples, or general residents.

| Paper | Why dropped |

| [W3015603533] Taiwanese PARO depression study | Participants were older adults with depression. The abstract doesn't mention dementia. |
